passage:
Dear Lalremsiami,
Sorry for the three-word reply yesterday: "Ok. Later. Bye." I wasn't being rude, I promise.
Here's what my day looked like. Six hours of physics revision, then deciding which chapters to drop, which sample paper to try, whether to join the group call. By nine my brain felt like a wrung-out cloth. Mummy asked what I wanted for dinner and I said "anything", then ate two packets of chips standing at the kitchen shelf.
Your message came right then, a long one about your school trip, and I couldn't think of a proper answer. So I typed the quickest thing.
I'll write properly on Sunday, when I haven't already made a hundred choices.
Love,
Damini

qa.q: What did Damini eat at the kitchen shelf?
qa.a: Damini ate two packets of chips standing at the kitchen shelf.

qa.q: Why did the quickest reply feel like the only option to Damini that night?
qa.a: After six hours of revision and many small decisions, Damini's brain felt like a wrung-out cloth, so thinking up a real answer felt beyond reach.

qa.q: What could Damini change on exam days so the evening goes better?
qa.a: Damini could settle dinner and which papers to try the night before, and keep an easy, healthier snack ready so tired choices are already made.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt on getting 'Ok. Later. Bye.'?
qa.a: Lalremsiami may have felt brushed off after writing a long, excited message, which is why the letter's explanation matters.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, worn out by revision and many decisions, reaches for junk food and sends a curt reply.

passage:
You know what happened yesterday, Tarun? I'd been at the library since eight. Twelve hours. Choosing which topics first, which notes to trust, whether to redo the mock test.
By the time I walked out, I was done. Home had texted: "Nilesh, dinner at home or tiffin from the canteen?" I didn't even answer. I bought a huge packet of spicy chips and a cold drink from the stall and ate them on the bus.
Then the teacher's email about choosing a project partner came, and I just replied "whatever works". Now I'm stuck with the one person who never shows up.
Honestly, it wasn't a decision. It was like my brain handed the wheel to whoever was nearest.

qa.q: How long had Nilesh been at the library?
qa.a: Twelve hours, since eight in the morning.

qa.q: What does 'my brain handed the wheel to whoever was nearest' suggest about how Nilesh felt?
qa.a: Nilesh felt too drained to steer anything, so the easiest option simply won, whether chips on the bus or 'whatever works'.

qa.q: What small step could stop Nilesh's worst choices on long study days?
qa.a: Nilesh could delay any reply that matters, like the partner email, until the next morning, and carry a proper dinner plan so the bus stall isn't the default.

qa.q: What was it like for the person at home who texted about dinner?
qa.a: They got no answer at all, so they may have waited, cooked for nothing, or worried about where Nilesh was.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after a long day of study decisions, grabs junk food and gives a careless reply to an important question.

passage:
I'm Gargi, and I share a room with my older sister Neelam, whose board exams are this month. Here's what I see.
In the morning she's careful. She plans the day in a notebook, picks the right pens, even chooses a proper breakfast. But by evening, after eight hours of papers, she's different.
Yesterday Papa asked if she wanted rice or roti, and she said "whatever" without looking up. Then she ate half a packet of cream biscuits from the cupboard for dinner. When her friend messaged about the study group, she sent a thumbs-up and later couldn't remember what she'd agreed to.
I don't know exactly what's in her head. She just looks like someone with nothing left.

qa.q: What did Neelam eat for dinner yesterday?
qa.a: She ate half a packet of cream biscuits from the cupboard.

qa.q: Why might 'whatever' have felt like the easiest answer for Neelam in the evening?
qa.a: After eight hours of papers and a day of careful planning, she seemed to have no energy left for even small choices, so any answer that ended the question felt best.

qa.q: How could Neelam plan her evenings during exams?
qa.a: She could decide dinner and study-group plans in the morning, while she is still careful, and leave evenings for rest.

qa.q: How does Gargi see the change in Neelam from morning to evening?
qa.a: Gargi notices the careful morning sister and the worn-out evening one, and seems concerned but unsure what Neelam is thinking.

grounding: A younger sibling observes a teen who plans carefully in the morning but, after hours of study, takes whatever is easiest.

passage:
Monday, 4 p.m.: Mehak had been solving chemistry papers since seven in the morning, choosing which chapter next, which answers to recheck, which doubts to leave for later. When her cousin Sonali messaged, "Want to split the bio notes? 🙂", Mehak typed "k" and went back to staring at the page. At the corner shop she grabbed two packets of chips and a cold drink without looking at anything else.
Wednesday, 3 p.m.: After lunch and her fifth past paper, she felt the same pull toward the shop. This time she didn't decide anything. She opened the note she had written at breakfast: "After study: banana, water, one walk round the block."
Friday, noon: Mehak met Sonali before the long afternoon session, while her head still felt clear. They planned the bio notes properly, and her reply that evening was a full message with a list.

qa.q: What did Mehak buy at the corner shop on Monday?
qa.a: She grabbed two packets of chips and a cold drink without looking at anything else.

qa.q: Why did replying "k" to Sonali feel reasonable to Mehak on Monday?
qa.a: After nine hours of choosing chapters, answers and doubts, even a small reply felt like one more decision, so the shortest one seemed like all she could manage.

qa.q: Which choice on Wednesday turned things around for Mehak, and why did it work?
qa.a: She followed the note she had written at breakfast instead of deciding in a tired moment, so the snack was already chosen while her mind was fresh.

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt reading that "k" on Monday compared with Friday's reply?
qa.a: On Monday Sonali may have wondered whether Mehak was annoyed or didn't want to work together; Friday's full message with a list would show that Mehak did care about the plan.

grounding: A teenager worn down by hours of study choices grabs junk snacks and sends a one-letter reply, then eases the pull by deciding things in advance.

passage: Nikita, put the pen down for a minute and listen to your Tanuja Mausi. The year of my Class 12 exams, I studied in the back room of our house in Kanpur from dawn. Every hour was a choice: this formula or that one, redo the sum or move on, which chapter to risk skipping. By evening your Nani would call, "Tanu, dal-rice or shall I make parathas?" and I'd snap, "Anything!" Then I'd finish a whole tin of namkeen standing by the shelf. One night my best friend asked me to join her revision group, and I said no without even thinking. I regretted that for weeks. My father noticed all this. He started asking me the important questions at breakfast, and he left a plate of fruit on my desk by five. You've been choosing since six this morning. Leave the group messages for tomorrow. Eat the orange first.

qa.q: Where did Tanuja study for her Class 12 exams?
qa.a: In the back room of her family's house in Kanpur, from dawn.

qa.q: How did the young Tanuja feel by evening during her Class 12 exams, and what shows it?
qa.a: Tanuja felt drained and irritable after choosing all day between formulas, sums and chapters, snapping "Anything!" at her mother and eating a whole tin of namkeen.

qa.q: Which change made by Tanuja's father was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: He moved the important questions to breakfast and left fruit on her desk by five, so she decided things while fresh and didn't have to pick a snack when worn out.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's best friend have taken that quick "no" to the revision group?
qa.a: The friend probably took it as a real rejection, not knowing Tanuja was simply too drained that evening to think it through.

grounding: An aunt's memory of her exam year shows a teenager, tired from constant study choices, grabbing snacks and giving careless replies.

passage: By nine in the evening, Mateo had been at his desk in Valencia since lunch: three past chemistry papers, a history timeline, forty small decisions about what to revise next. When his mother called him for dinner, he said he wasn't hungry and grabbed a bag of crisps and a fizzy drink from the cupboard instead. Then his phone buzzed. Liam had sent a long message about splitting the biology project: who does the poster, who does the talk, which days to meet. Mateo stared at it. His brain felt like wet cardboard. He typed "whatever u want" and threw the phone on the bed. An hour later, Liam replied: "ok, u do the talk then." Mateo groaned. He hated giving talks. On any other evening, he'd have said so.

qa.q: What did Liam's long message ask about?
qa.a: It was about splitting the biology project: who does the poster, who does the talk, and which days to meet.

qa.q: Why did Mateo reply 'whatever u want'?
qa.a: Mateo felt drained and foggy after hours of choosing what to revise, so one more decision felt too heavy and the easiest reply won.

qa.q: What could Mateo do the next time a big choice arrives at the end of a long study day?
qa.a: He could reply that he will answer in the morning, and eat a proper meal before deciding anything.

qa.q: How might Liam read 'whatever u want'?
qa.a: Liam might take it as real agreement, or feel brushed off, not knowing Mateo was simply exhausted.

grounding: Shows a teenager after hours of study grabbing junk snacks and sending a quick careless reply he later regrets.

passage: Exam week at the boarding school meant study hall from four to eight, no talking. When the bell finally rang, Francis stumbled to the mess, skipped the dal and sabzi, and piled his plate with fried papad and gulab jamun. At the table, Lakshmi slid a form across. "Elective choices. The warden wants them by nine." Last week Francis had spent an hour talking about taking Computer Science. Now the boxes swam in front of his eyes. "What did you pick?" "Geography." Francis ticked Geography and handed the form back without reading the rest. Lying in his dorm bed at ten, he sat up with a jolt. Geography? He hadn't wanted Geography at all. First thing in the morning, he went to the warden's office to ask for the form back.

qa.q: By what time did the warden want the elective forms?
qa.a: The warden wanted them by nine.

qa.q: Why did Francis just copy Lakshmi's choice?
qa.a: Francis felt tired and foggy after four hours in study hall, so copying was the easiest option and his own wish slipped away.

qa.q: What did Francis do the next morning, and what could prevent this next time?
qa.a: He went to the warden to ask for the form back; next time he could fill in important forms earlier in the day or ask for time to decide.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel if Francis asks why they picked the same subject?
qa.a: Lakshmi might feel surprised or a bit awkward, having only shared an answer, not meant to decide for Francis.

grounding: Shows a teenager, drained after long study hours, grabbing fried snacks and copying a friend's elective choice.

passage:
Dear Rukmini didi,
You asked how board prep is going, so here's the honest version. The studying is fine. It's the evenings that are the problem. I sit from seven in the morning, and by six I've made about a hundred little decisions: which chapter, which sample paper, redo this sum or move on. After that, I'm useless. Yesterday Amma asked if I wanted rice or rotis, and I snapped, "I don't care, just give me something!" Then I ate a whole packet of namkeen standing in the kitchen and scrolled for an hour instead of eating dinner. Today, the same. I felt awful afterwards, because Amma had made my favourite.
How did you manage this in your boards? Did you have a trick for the evenings?
Your tired little sister,
Jaya

qa.q: What did Jaya eat standing in the kitchen?
qa.a: Jaya ate a whole packet of namkeen.

qa.q: Why did Jaya snap at Amma over rice or rotis?
qa.a: Jaya felt drained and irritable after a hundred study decisions, so even an easy question about dinner felt like too much.

qa.q: What could help Jaya's evenings go better?
qa.a: Planning the next day's study the night before, letting Amma choose dinner without asking, and asking Rukmini didi what worked in her boards.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when Jaya snapped and skipped dinner?
qa.a: Amma might have felt hurt, having made Jaya's favourite, and perhaps worried about how tired Jaya is.

grounding: Shows a teenager so worn down by a day of study decisions that evenings bring snapping and junk snacks.

passage: So you want to know about the chips thing? Okay. I'm Divyansh, and during board prep last March I studied from six in the morning till almost nine at night. By evening my brain was porridge. My sister Lakshmi would ask, "Dal or khichdi for dinner?" and I'd just say "whatever." Then I'd open the cupboard and eat a whole packet of masala chips standing up. Friends texted me real questions, like whether to join the group revision on Sunday, and I'd send a thumbs-up without reading properly. Twice I agreed to things I didn't want. Lakshmi finally noticed and started asking me the big stuff at breakfast, when I could still think. Honestly, that helped more than any timetable.

qa.q: What did Divyansh eat standing up in the evenings?
qa.a: Divyansh ate a whole packet of masala chips standing up.

qa.q: Why did saying "whatever" and sending a thumbs-up feel reasonable to Divyansh at night?
qa.a: After studying from six till nine Divyansh felt drained and foggy, so any choice felt like one too many and the easiest option brought relief.

qa.q: What small change could protect Divyansh's choices during exam weeks?
qa.a: Keep real questions for the morning, as Lakshmi began doing, and decide simple dinner and snack options earlier in the day so evening choices are already made.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt when Divyansh kept answering "whatever"?
qa.a: Lakshmi may have felt brushed off at first, then worried, which is why Lakshmi moved the big questions to breakfast.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after long study hours, grabs junk snacks and gives quick replies because choosing has worn them out.

passage:
Monday. Aditi finished her physics mock at noon, planned the whole week's revision, picked which chapters to redo, chose a new pen colour for each subject and felt oddly powerful.

Wednesday. After three more hours of past papers, her cousin Tanuja asked which film they should watch on Saturday. Aditi stared at the list, said "you pick," then ordered a sugary cold coffee she didn't even like and snapped at the delivery man for being late.

Friday. Aditi tried something Tanuja suggested: she wrote tomorrow's lunch, study order and one fun thing on a sticky note before breakfast. That evening she followed the note without arguing with herself and slept earlier than she had all week.

qa.q: What did Aditi write on the sticky note on Friday?
qa.a: She wrote tomorrow's lunch, study order and one fun thing.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling on Wednesday when she said "you pick" and snapped at the delivery man?
qa.a: She was worn out and irritable after hours of past papers, so even choosing a film felt like a burden and she grabbed the quickest option.

qa.q: Which choice worked on Friday, and why?
qa.a: Deciding small things in the morning worked because Aditi used her fresh energy for them and did not have to choose again when she was tired.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see the change in Aditi between Wednesday and Friday?
qa.a: Tanuja probably felt snubbed on Wednesday and then glad on Friday to see Aditi calmer and easier to be around.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after many choices on exam days, falls back on quick, easy options until planning small decisions ahead helps.

passage: Sit, Sarita, and let your Ama Dolma tell you something before your exams. When I was a girl of sixteen in Darjeeling, we had the school leaving exams in winter. I studied by the stove from dawn, choosing which chapter, which notes, which question to try first. By evening I could not decide anything. My mother would ask, "Tea with salt or sugar?" and I would just take whatever was nearest. One night I bought three packets of sweets from the corner shop with my bus money and walked home in the cold. My teacher saw me yawning and said, "Make your hard choices before lunch, Dolma." So I did. The evenings became simple: same meal, same walk, bed. My marks were not perfect, but my head was clearer.

qa.q: What did Dolma buy with the bus money one night?
qa.a: Dolma bought three packets of sweets from the corner shop.

qa.q: Why did buying the sweets feel reasonable to young Dolma at the time?
qa.a: After a whole day of choosing chapters and questions Dolma felt exhausted, and the sweets were an easy comfort that needed no thinking.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Dolma's evenings?
qa.a: Dolma's teacher told her to make hard choices before lunch, and after that Dolma kept her evenings simple with the same meal, walk and bedtime.

qa.q: How might Dolma's mother have seen her daughter during those exam weeks?
qa.a: Dolma's mother may have been puzzled and a little concerned that Dolma could not even pick salt or sugar in her tea.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a teenager in exam season, hours of choosing left her grabbing easy sweets and not deciding.

passage:
It was the night before the chemistry board exam, and Aparna had been choosing all day: which chapter first, which questions to skip, whether to redo organic or trust it. At nine the power went out, and she kept going by the dim inverter light.
Gurleen messaged: "Can you send me your polymer notes? Please? 🙏"
Aparna, who usually wrote long, careful replies, typed "no" and turned the phone over.
In the kitchen she ignored the dal Amma had kept warm and ate half a packet of chips standing up.
Ten minutes later, still crunching, she felt awful. She picked up the phone again. "Sorry, brain fried. Sending photos now. Good luck ❤️"
Then she put the chips away, sat down with the dal and closed the textbook for the night.

qa.q: What did Gurleen ask Aparna for?
qa.a: Gurleen asked for Aparna's polymer notes.

qa.q: Why did Aparna reply just 'no'?
qa.a: Aparna felt drained and irritable after a whole day of study decisions, so a quick, easy answer was all she had left.

qa.q: What did Aparna do after ten minutes that helped?
qa.a: Aparna apologised, sent the notes, ate the dal and stopped studying for the night, giving a tired brain some rest.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt on getting a one-word 'no'?
qa.a: Gurleen may have felt hurt and surprised, since Aparna usually wrote long, careful replies.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after hours of study decisions, grabs whatever is easiest, a curt reply and junk snacks.

passage:
The half-yearly maths paper ended at noon, and after it the Class 10 students had to fill in elective forms, vote for house captains and pick places for the farewell photo. By four, Bidisha's head felt like cotton wool.
At the bus stop outside the school in Salt Lake, Karthik caught up with her, waving a list. "We need a science project topic by tonight. Solar ovens, water filters or the bird survey?"
"Whatever. The first one," Bidisha said, without looking.
"You hate solar ovens. You said so last week."
"I don't care. Just pick."
On the bus she bought a packet of spicy peanuts she didn't even like, because the seller held it right in front of her.
At home, after a nap and tea, she messaged Karthik: "Wait. Bird survey. Obviously bird survey. Sorry, I was dead at four."

qa.q: What three project topics did Karthik offer?
qa.a: Solar ovens, water filters or the bird survey.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha say 'whatever' at the bus stop?
qa.a: Bidisha felt drained and foggy after the exam and all the forms, so any choice felt like too much effort.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do next time a decision comes after a draining day?
qa.a: Bidisha could say she'll reply after a rest, since the nap and tea showed she chooses better when refreshed.

qa.q: How does Karthik see Bidisha's first answer?
qa.a: Karthik is puzzled and a bit concerned, knowing Bidisha hates solar ovens.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after an exam and many decisions, grabs whatever is easiest until rest restores her judgement.

passage:
"Okay, we've done three papers today," Dilnaz said, stretching in the hostel reading room. "Pizza or the mess thali?"
"Pizza," Vidya said instantly.
"You said this morning you'd eat properly this week."
"That was this morning. This morning I had a brain."
"And your mum's message about the bus ticket for Sunday?"
"I'll just book the first one. Whatever."
"The first one is at five a.m."
Vidya groaned and put her head on the table. "I can't choose anything else today. Every decision feels like lifting a sofa."
Dilnaz slid the phone away from her. "Then don't. Thali, because it's already paid for. Bus ticket tomorrow, after breakfast. Deal?"
"Deal," Vidya mumbled into the table.

qa.q: How many papers had they done that day?
qa.a: They had done three papers that day.

qa.q: Why did Vidya pick pizza and the first bus instantly?
qa.a: Vidya felt exhausted after three papers, and every decision felt like lifting a sofa, so she grabbed the easiest option.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Taking the already-paid thali and booking the bus after breakfast, so a tired brain didn't have to make real choices.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see Vidya's instant choices?
qa.a: Dilnaz sees them as tiredness rather than real preferences, and gently steps in to help.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after a day of exam study, grabs easy options for food and travel because choosing feels too heavy.

passage:
Last Tuesday, in the middle of the winter prelims, I did something I'm still a bit ashamed of. I had spent six hours on physics numericals at the dining table while fog pressed against the window. By eight my brain felt like wet paper.
Payal, my little sister, asked, "Ganga Didi, roti or the khichdi Mumma left?" I couldn't decide, so I tore open a family packet of chips and ate it standing at the fridge.
Then my friend Tanvi sent three photos of dresses for her cousin's wedding. "Which one?? Help!!" I typed "whatever u like" and turned the phone face down.
In the morning, after sleep and a proper breakfast, I saw her reply: "ok 🙁". It wasn't that I didn't care. I had simply run out of choosing.

qa.q: What did Ganga eat instead of choosing between roti and khichdi?
qa.a: She tore open a family packet of chips and ate it standing at the fridge.

qa.q: Why did the chips and the quick reply feel like the only choices Ganga could make that evening?
qa.a: After six hours of numericals Ganga felt drained, with a brain "like wet paper", so anything that needed a decision felt too heavy and the easiest option won.

qa.q: What could Ganga try on the next long study day?
qa.a: She could settle dinner and reply to friends during an afternoon break, or tell friends she'll answer properly after sleep.

qa.q: How might Tanvi have felt reading "whatever u like"?
qa.a: Tanvi may have felt brushed off and a little hurt, since she was excited about the dresses and wanted Ganga's help 🙁

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after hours of study, grabs junk food and sends a quick reply because choosing has worn her out.
